title: The cost of each side condition in a gauged logical measurement
abstract: A logical measurement reads out protected information, and the noise it survives sets how much a quantum computation can absorb. Gauging builds one from a graph on the measured qubits, one extra qubit on each edge, turning a global operator into local parity checks. Its tolerance splits in two: the distance of the code left behind, and the rounds a fault can hide in. Williamson and Yoder proved both components stay at or above the code's distance. The guarantee rests on four side conditions taken as a package, none of them priced. Here we show they are not worth the same: the demand that the first and last rounds be perfect, which reads like bookkeeping, carries the temporal part. Dropping it flattens the fault distance, the least weight of a fault that passes unseen and flips the readout, to one for every code and round count, in a model whose detectors compare adjacent rounds; the full protocol collapses on the instance measured. The expansion condition, that no small set of qubits be sealed off, does not decide the outcome: two paths on the same qubits, both outside the covered regime, give distances one and two. The round count is tight where comparing rounds is the whole rule; the full protocol reaches the distance a round early. Both components are computed exactly on a gauged bivariate bicycle code and a Bacon--Shor measurement, inside a proof assistant. Threshold estimates consume such numbers; side conditions can be priced.
summary: This paper rigorously analyzes the overhead and necessary assumptions (side conditions) required to guarantee fault tolerance in quantum computation via gauged logical measurements. It demonstrates that these conditions are not equally important, providing a 'pricing' mechanism for design choices. This work refines the theoretical understanding of error correction by pinpointing which assumptions are essential for maintaining computational integrity.
main_problem: The paper determines the precise cost associated with various side conditions required for a fault-tolerant gauged logical measurement in quantum computation.
main_result: The authors show that the four necessary side conditions are not equally costly; dropping the requirement that the first and last rounds are perfect causes the fault distance to collapse significantly.
method: The analysis uses graph theory, algebraic topology (e.g., 1-cosystolic distance), and rigorous proof assistants to analyze the structure of error detection checks.
model_or_system: The model is quantum computation employing logical measurements, which are implemented by 'gauging' a global logical operator into local parity checks using an auxiliary graph built on the measured qubits.
key_observables: Fault-tolerance distance (spatial and temporal components), weight of undetectable faults, and the status of four side conditions (C1-C4).
important_parameters: Code distance, number of rounds ($T$), and the structure of the auxiliary graph.
main_assumptions: The initial guarantee rests on four side conditions; the analysis critically examines which of these assumptions are truly necessary for the fault-tolerance bound.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the auxiliary graph, cuts on the graph, and the two components of the fault distance: spatial checks (deformed code) and temporal checks (round comparison).
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the fault-tolerance guarantee, deriving bounds based on graph cuts and temporal comparisons, culminating in a detailed 'axiom audit' to price the necessity of each side condition.
why_interesting: While highly abstract, the rigorous quantification of necessary assumptions in fault tolerance provides a blueprint for designing robust quantum protocols, which is foundational to quantum information science.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
